text:
Norman Swan: Hello and welcome to this week's Health Report with me,
Norman Swann. Today there are 80,000 Australians who have an easily
diagnosed high genetic risk of cancer. They don't know it, and we need to do
something about it.

Ian Frayling: The little light comes on in your car with the oil light. Your airbus
will scream at you if you try to land with the wheels up, and your phone will tell
you when it's your anniversary tomorrow—it's life and death, right? So we have
to use technology simply to find these things and tell people what to do when
they need to do it.

Norman Swan: A world first for Australian research—a simple blood test, a so-
called liquid biopsy for cancer which saves having more expensive, painful and
less accurate tests.

How lung problems in women are different and doctors need to know about it, not
to mention women. And how you may not need to pay a fortune for brain training
programs to keep your mind fit. Some simple, cheap activities may be all you
need. At least according to a large study which has found a reduced instance of
what's called mild cognitive impairment, which can be the first step for some
people towards dementia. The lead author was Yonas Geda of the Mayo Clinic in
the United States.

Yonas Geda: Several groups of investigators, including ourselves, have reported
a cross-sectional association between mentally stimulating activities and
decreased odds of having mild cognitive impairment.

Norman Swan: And when you say cross-sectional, this means like a snapshot.

Yonas Geda: Yes.

Norman Swan: If you just take a snapshot in time, people who do mentally
stimulating activities seem to have better thinking and memory ability. But it
doesn't tell you whether or not it's cause and effect.

Yonas Geda: Exactly.

Norman Swan: So they could be doing these mentally stimulating activities
because they can rather than because it's helping them.
 
Yonas Geda: Exactly. So what we did is we published a cross-sectional study.
We looked at about ten mentally stimulating activities. We observed that five of
them are strongly associated with decreased odds of having MCI. So we took
those five…

Norman Swan: MCI being mild cognitive impairment.

Yonas Geda: Intermediate stage between normal ageing and dementia. So we
took those five mentally stimulating activities…

Norman Swan: What were they?

Yonas Geda: Reading books, playing games (when we say games, simple
games, board games), craft activities such as knitting, computer use (simple
email, browsing), and social activities. So we took these five and we tested it in a
prospective cohort study. We took about 2,000 people, 70 years and older.

Norman Swan: And just watched to see what happened to them…

Yonas Geda: Exactly. We followed them forward in time for an average of about
four years. And then we wanted to see…at baseline all of them are cognitively
normal, and then followed them forward in time and then tried to compare their
outcome of mild cognitive impairment between those who engage in mentally
stimulating activities versus those who don't.

Norman Swan: And what did you find?

Yonas Geda: Mentally stimulating activities, particularly craft activities, computer
use, social activities and playing games were associated with decreased risk of
having mild cognitive impairment.

Norman Swan: So this is the group as a whole…

Yonas Geda: Yes.

Norman Swan: And in fact when I look at your results, computer use really stood
out, the significance was much greater than the other activities.

Yonas Geda: Exactly. Computer use is top of the list, and again, we asked for
only simple computer use: email, browsing, that's it.
 
Norman Swan: And the social activities were what?

Yonas Geda: Doing group activities, going to theatres or going to a museum or
group activities such as Bible studying.

Norman Swan: Okay, so then you decided to look at it via genetic risk, using this
gene called APOE ε4, which does confer an increased risk of cognitive
impairment.

Yonas Geda: Particularly Alzheimer's. So we wanted to know, if I am a carrier of
the genetic risk, and if I still engage in reading books, I will have slightly
decreased risk of having MCI, even if I have genetic risk. Even if I have the
genetic risk, these mentally stimulating activities seem to confer some degree of
decreased risk for MCI as well.

Norman Swan: So what you're saying is then that these five activities—
particularly craft activities, computer use and social activities—those will protect
you to some extent if you're carrying this high risk gene.

Yonas Geda: 'To some extent' is a very good qualifier. If you don't have it, the
benefit is even more.

Norman Swan: So given that most people don't know their APOE ε4 status, the
bottom line is what?

Yonas Geda: The bottom line is that this paper, honestly, it gives hope. We
looked at very simple activities, accessible to anyone above age 70. We didn't
look at fancy gadgets, fancy games. And what we observed is that even if a
person starts mentally stimulating activities even in late life, after age 70 the
person starts these activities, there is reasonable chance to decrease the risk of
incident MCI by simply engaging in these accessible, simple mentally stimulating
activities.

Norman Swan: What sort of dose of these activities do people have to be doing?
Because if they were having an effect, more might be better. So how much of this
were they doing, and did you factor in—if you like to use a medical term—the
dose of these activities?
 
Yonas Geda: Anywhere from two days per week and then above we have
observed benefit.

Norman Swan: You mean twice a week for how long?

Yonas Geda: Even as small as twice a week for a year.

Norman Swan: On the computer for an hour a day, two hours a day—what?

Yonas Geda: Oh, actually unfortunately we didn't look at how many hours of
computer in one sitting. Unfortunately we didn't look at that one. But in general
we looked at number of activities per week. Engaging in any of these activities
about two times minimum per week seems to be associated with decreased risk.

Norman Swan: Yonas Geda, thank you very much for joining us on the Health
Report.

Yonas Geda: You are very welcome, and I look forward to listen to it.

Norman Swan: New listeners to the Health Report are always welcome. Yonas
Geda is Professor of Psychiatry and Neurology at the Mayo Clinic.

Eighty thousand Australians are estimated to have a genetic abnormality which
puts them at increased risk of a number of malignancies, especially bowel
cancer, and they don't know it. It's said that some carriers have up to a 75%
chance of developing cancer by the age of 70. It's called Lynch syndrome, and
as we speak, a report is being released calling for widespread testing. One of the
people involved is Ian Frayling, a British expert on Lynch syndrome, who's a
genetic pathologist at the University Hospital of Wales in Cardiff. I spoke to Ian
earlier.

Ian, thank you for joining us on the Health Report.

Ian Frayling: Pleasure.

Norman Swan: So 5% of people are actually only diagnosed with Lynch
syndrome. You'd better tell us the sort of cancers that Lynch syndrome's
associated with.
 
Ian Frayling: Well, it was first identified on the basis of predisposing to bowel
and endometrial, so that's womb cancer.

Norman Swan: Uterus.

Ian Frayling: Yeah, uterus, as well as to some extent gastric cancers like
stomach cancer. But it causes a whole variety, we now understand, about 12
different types and counting. There's a relatively low risk of ovarian cancer, but
also gall bladder, small bowel cancer, bile duct cancer, cancer of the ducts that
come down from the kidney, which is otherwise quite unusual. Young onset
bladder cancer, some brain cancers.

Norman Swan: So how would you know that there might be Lynch syndrome in
your family?

Ian Frayling: Well that's incredibly difficult for both professionals and members of
the public. Most people are familiar with familial breast/ovarian cancer, where it's
breast and ovary, largely.

Norman Swan: And in young women, relatively young women.

Ian Frayling: Yeah, it tends to occur in younger people.

Norman Swan: But that's true in Lynch syndrome as well.

Ian Frayling: That's true in Lynch…

Norman Swan: Are we talking about diagnosis under 50?

Ian Frayling: Well, about a third of cases of Lynch produce cancer below the age
of 50 in the bowel, about a third between 50 and 65, and a third over 65. So
you're never too young and you're never too old.

Norman Swan: So there's not really a reliable way of telling from your family
history.

Ian Frayling: No. It's more likely if it's younger, but it's not an absolute.

Norman Swan: And do you know, if you say to somebody, look bowel cancer
runs in my family. does that tell you if you're at risk?
 
Ian Frayling: That can do. The problem is that we've come at this from the
direction of spotting bowel cancer in families, but we now understand, because it
causes so many other cancers, that we can't be so selective. And in fact the
family history is useful but it's not the best way of finding it.

Norman Swan: And what's going wrong here, it's what's called a mismatch
repair gene, the DNA doesn't repair itself the way it would do in somebody who
doesn't have Lynch syndrome.

Ian Frayling: Yeah. The genes that are responsible for causing Lynch syndrome
are involved in the process of DNA repair in cells. And cells are very careful
things. They won't divide unless their DNA is repaired. So if you damage the
mechanism for mending DNA cells can divide in an unruly fashion. But there's
emerging evidence which is very exciting that perhaps there's another pathway to
cancer in Lynch syndrome hitherto undiscovered.

Norman Swan: Oh really, and that could end up with understanding better
treatments?

Ian Frayling: Absolutely. What all this study of familial bowel cancer in all its
different forms is telling us is that it's not a simple process. There's many different
ways to a bowel cancer.

Norman Swan: Now, the BRCA1 gene, breast cancer, is relatively rare, and it
follows ethnic groups like Ashkenazi Jews…or do you disagree with that?

Ian Frayling: Well, no, no, there are founder mutations for every genetic
condition on the planet.

Norman Swan: Once upon a time in the Ashkenazi Jewish population somebody
got that mutation and because it was in a closed community it spread.

Ian Frayling: Absolutely, kept it within themselves.

Norman Swan: And what about Lynch syndrome, is there any ethnic
identification, and is it that rare?

Ian Frayling: It's actually probably more common that familial breast/ovarian
cancer. It could be up to twice as common, but we get five times less referrals for
 
it than familial breast/ovarian. So there's a complete skewing against Lynch
syndrome because it's difficult to spot, members of the public find it difficult to
realise they're in a family situation, doctors don't understand it…

Norman Swan: But let's say you get the diagnosis, and we'll come to testing in a
moment, what do you do? Bowel cancer is fairly obvious, you can have regular
colonoscopies or faecal occult blood testing. But uterine cancer, biliary tract
cancer? These are not easy cancers to screen for or detect…

Ian Frayling: No.

Norman Swan: Is there a drug you can take that helps the mismatch?

Ian Frayling: We did a trial where we tried using aspirin in individuals with Lynch,
and it showed a remarkable result, that it seemed to be extremely effective at
preventing a large proportion of all the cancers they get, not just the bowel
cancers. We're now in the process of organising a trial around the world where
we're trying to find out the best dose of aspirin.

Norman Swan: Now, Monday evening, Australian time, launching a report which
calls for testing for Lynch syndrome. Who's going to get tested and how would
that happen, a screening program?

Ian Frayling: Hopefully in parallel with what the National Institute for Health and
Care Excellence in the UK has just authorised, which is that all bowel cancers in
the United Kingdom now must be tested to see if they're due to Lynch syndrome.
Based on the work we're doing at Cancer Council New South Wales, what we're
urging for is that a similar situation should pertain in Australia, and that when a
pathologist finds evidence of Lynch in a bowel cancer, which is done by a couple
of pretty standard tests now, that initiates a referral to the local clinical genetics
department, and the individual and their family can then be cared for
appropriately.

Norman Swan: So it's not the whole population, it's just that basically all bowel
cancer specimens should be tested for it and that's the red light that gets the
family tested and you can start doing what you have to do.
 
Ian Frayling: Yeah. It may also similarly be worth testing cases of endometrial
cancer and, for example, small bowel and gall bladder because they're so
characteristic.

Norman Swan: Can you afford it?

Ian Frayling: You can't afford not to do it. In the health economic analysis we did
in the UK, we showed that it was hugely worthwhile testing certainly the young
onset cases. It was worthwhile testing every case of bowel cancer up to the age
of 70, and NICE decided it was worth simply testing everybody. It was simpler to
advise that every bowel cancer get tested. If I can summarise a 500-page report
that we did in the UK down to a one-liner and trying to convert to Australian
dollars—you don't have to prevent many $65,000 bowel cancers to pay for a hell
of a lot of $100 tests and $500 colonoscopies.

Norman Swan: Ian Frayling, we'll watch this with interest. Thanks very much for
joining us.

Ian Frayling: Thank you Norman.

Norman Swan: And I must declare an interest in colorectal issues as the proud
owner of an occasional polyp. Ian Frayling is a genetic pathologist at the
University Hospital of Wales in Cardiff.

A liquid biopsy is like something out of Star Trek, an almost painless way to
diagnose disease without taking out large lumps of tissue surgically. A wife and
husband team at Peter MacCallum Cancer Centre in Melbourne have developed
a world first liquid biopsy for blood cancers like leukaemia, which may avoid
painful, expensive bone marrow biopsies. Sarah-Jane and Mark Dawson are in
our Melbourne studio. Welcome to the Health Report.

Sarah-Jane Dawson: Thank you for having us, Norman.

Mark Dawson: Thank you.

Norman Swan: Sarah, you were at Cambridge for ten years and you've now
decamped to the Palace on Parkville, the new Victorian Comprehensive Cancer
Centre.
 
Sarah-Jane Dawson: That's right, I'm from Melbourne originally, and did my
medical training here in Melbourne but then went to the University of Cambridge
and studied over there, did a PhD and some post-doctoral research over there,
and developed these skills that I've now brought back to Melbourne and more
specifically to Peter MacCallum Cancer Centre and the Victorian Comprehensive
Cancer Centre.

Norman Swan: Before we get to the blood cancers that you and Mark have
worked on, you yourself have developed liquid biopsies for solid tumours like
breast cancer. What is a liquid biopsy?

Sarah-Jane Dawson: Yes, so essentially a liquid biopsy is a test that measures
something called circulating tumour DNA. So we know that most cancer types
can actually release small, tiny fragments of cancer DNA into a patient's
bloodstream. And we now have quite sophisticated ways with which we can
measure these small amounts of circulating tumour DNA, and in doing so learn
something about the cancer and how it's responding to treatment.

Norman Swan: More than you can learn from a straight biopsy by putting the
needle in the tumour?

Sarah-Jane Dawson: Yes, so one of the advantages is this testing is based on a
blood test, so a blood test can certainly be repeated more frequently during
someone's cancer treatment compared to an invasive tissue biopsy. You know,
there are several limitations of tissue biopsies, they're invasive and quite
challenging for patients…

Norman Swan: You might miss the spot as well.

Sarah-Jane Dawson: That's right, yeah, they're only biopsy-ing a single area of
the tumour and we know that heterogeneity within cancers is a problem: no
single area of a tumour is the same. So the liquid biopsy alternative may be more
comprehensive. Certainly it allows us to see DNA that's been shed into the
bloodstream from all of the different sites of the tumour.

Norman Swan: Mark, tell us about this one for blood tumours. What are we
talking about here, leukaemia?
 
Mark Dawson: So the two major cancers that we've studied here are a disease
called chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, and another precursor condition called
myelodysplastic syndrome. So if we start with the latter, the latter is really a
problem of the production factory for our blood cells, which is the bone marrow.
And so…

Norman Swan: And you really teeter on a knife-edge of leukaemia when you've
got MDS.

Mark Dawson: Correct, that's exactly right, Norman. And really here the quality
and quantity of the cells that are being produced is not adequate. But this is
actually a relatively common disease that is quite difficult to diagnose, because
there are a number of different everyday exposures that may give rise to low
blood counts: infections, some of the toxins that we consume such as alcohol,
and other toxic exposures as well. So it's not always clear whether the low blood
counts are caused by a cancer. But all cancers, as you've just been talking
about, have a somatic or acquired mutation in their DNA. And essentially that's
what we look for, we look for an abnormality that says that the cells are
cancerous. We do that currently with a bone marrow biopsy, but what our results
suggest is that we may be able to do that effectively with the liquid biopsy.

Norman Swan: Sarah-Jane, tests have a chequered history; people tout them
with great hype and then you find that they're inaccurate. It depends on the
person who's doing the test whether or not you get a positive result or not.
They're horribly expensive and in the end may not tell you any more than you get
from the traditional test. How reliable and affordable are these liquid biopsies?

Sarah-Jane Dawson: This is not a new field. We've known for quite some time
that it's possible to find these small traces of cancer DNA in the bloodstream of
patients with cancer. But what's changed recently is improvement in technology.
We now have improvements in the way that we can reliably detect these small
amounts of DNA. So these tests are now much more sensitive than they have
been previously and this has really seen great growth and expansion of research
in this area.

Norman Swan: Are they ready for show time yet, or is it still experimental?
 
Sarah-Jane Dawson: We're certainly working very hard to now start to make
these tests more readily available for patients and we're hoping to be in a
situation to be able to do that in the next few months.

Norman Swan: And affordably?

Sarah-Jane Dawson: Yes. The costs of these tests are actually likely to be very
affordable for patients. They're still not covered by government subsidies but the
hope is in the future that the more patients that have access to these tests, then
they may actually be reimbursed.

Norman Swan: Mark, I want to talk to you about a paper you've just published
in Science magazine, one of the world's most prestigious journals—although you
and Sarah-Jane have also published in a very prestigious journal for your liquid
biopsy—on epigenetics and cancer and the opportunities for treatment we should
just talk about. So this is an extraordinary…it's not that new an area, but this is
stuff that happens around the outside of DNA rather than inside it itself.

Mark Dawson: That's right, Norman. So epigenetics I often describe using a very
common sight that is very familiar to everyone and that happens in nature; how a
caterpillar becomes a butterfly. These two look very, very different but essentially
their DNA, their blueprint…

Norman Swan: The genes are identical…

Mark Dawson: …it's absolutely identical. What is different is what pages of that
instruction manual are read to give rise to a caterpillar or a butterfly. And that
ability to be able to access the DNA at the right place at the right time, to be able
to repair it and replicate it, that process, and the proteins that control that
process, is the study of epigenetics.

Norman Swan: And to what extent is it involved in cancer?

Mark Dawson: What we've learned over the last ten years as we've been
sequencing lots of genomes of patients with cancer is that mutations in genes
that code for epigenetic regulators are probably the most frequently occurring
class of mutations in cancer. And this really shouldn't be…
 
Norman Swan: Just to be totally mind-bending, you're not talking about
mutations that directly cause the cancer, you're talking about mutations that
actually change the shape of the DNA and how it works.

Mark Dawson: No, it's a bit of both. So if we think of the proteins that change the
way we access our DNA we call these epigenetic proteins. The genes that code
for these epigenetic proteins are what is mutated in cancer. And this really makes
the genome much more plastic and more malleable, because when you mutate
these things you are suddenly able to keep genes on that should be turned off
with normal development. And similarly you sometimes turn off genes that would
come over to protect the cell, come on to protect a cell should something bad
happen. So mutations in epigenetic regulators are extremely common…

Norman Swan: So which kind of tumours are we talking about here?.

Mark Dawson: Virtually all tumours. Most tumours that've been sequenced have
been found to have mutations in epigenetic regulators.

Norman Swan: And what does it mean for treatment?

Mark Dawson: What it means for treatment is that we now have a new way of
trying to manipulate the cell, trying to rewire this cell by finding therapies that
target these mutated epigenetic regulators that turn off these genes in the
specific cancer cells and try to make them more susceptible to the body's way of
clearing them, including the immune system.

Norman Swan: Existing drugs, or new drugs?

Mark Dawson: New drugs. There is a raft of new drugs that are being developed
to try and tug at the epigenome to reset cancer cells.

Norman Swan: And will these work hand in hand with existing drugs, or do they
want to do the job by themselves?

Mark Dawson: It's very unlikely that they will do the job by themselves. They're
going to need to be used as part of combination therapies. And the next decade
will involve just working out how best to use them.
 
Norman Swan: So Sarah-Jane, does your liquid biopsy pick up epigenetic
changes, or just the throw-off DNA that's caused by cancer?

Sarah-Jane Dawson: No, it certainly can pick up epigenetic changes as well,
such as DNA methylation. So there is a whole host of genetic changes that
studying the cancer DNA in the bloodstream can reveal.

Norman Swan: Thank you very much to you both. Impressed, you know, a joint
husband and wife or wife and husband lab doing such great work,
congratulations.

Both: Thank you very much.

Norman Swan: Sarah-Jane and Mark Dawson, of the Peter MacCallum Cancer
Centre, and as I say, the Palace on Parkville, the new Victorian Comprehensive
Cancer Centre. If you're not from Melbourne you should drive by, it's a very
impressive building.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a massive chronic health issue
in Australia. The image that's usually portrayed is of a breathless man coughing
his lungs out. But women develop COPD too, and according to a paper last week
from the George Institute in Sydney, women with COPD receive scant attention,
despite being more likely to die from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease than
breast and lung cancer combined. And it also behaves differently in women. The
lead author was head of the George Institute Respiratory Group, respiratory
physician Christine Jenkins, and she's in our Sydney studio. Welcome, Christine.

Christine Jenkins: Good afternoon, Norman.

Norman Swan: So just tell us what COPD is, because I kind of glanced over
that, given that you know better than me.

Christine Jenkins: Yes, it's not a term people are familiar with, but they probably
are familiar with the words chronic bronchitis and emphysema. And they are
really the community's understanding of this disease. It's a chronic lung disease
where the airways narrow because the lung tissue is destroyed by gases, dusts,
particles, noxious inhalations of which tobacco smoke is the most common in our
country, but not in the rest of the world.
 
Norman Swan: Indoor cooking and that sort of thing, indoor fires can cause the
problem.

Christine Jenkins: Most definitely. Biomass fuel exposure, we call it, people
who have to burn carbon-rich fuel for their heating and cooking in poorly
ventilated houses around the world very commonly develop COPD as well. So
this accounts for why women globally actually have the same prevalence of
COPD as men, whilst in our country actually COPD is slightly more common in
men, but because women now smoke as much as men do it's becoming equal
and prevalent.

Norman Swan: And to what extent is it a problem, what's the dimension of
COPD in Australia?

Christine Jenkins: About 7% to 8% of people have significant COPD, clinically
important COPD. If you look at it over the age range it increases in prevalence
from the age of about 55 through to 80+, and by the time people are in their 80s
COPD prevalence be up around 15%.

Norman Swan: That's a lot of people.

Christine Jenkins: It's a large number of people. And in fact there's an epidemic
of COPD around the world, so around 300 million people around the world have
COPD. In 1990 it was the sixth leading cause of death from chronic disease. In
2000 it was the fourth and in 2020 it will be the third.

Norman Swan: And what's different about it in women?

Christine Jenkins: In women it is significantly different in a range of ways. The
first way, and one very important way for people to know is that women appear to
need a much smaller exposure to a noxious substance such as smoking in order
to develop COPD. So, for instance…

Norman Swan: So a bigger risk with a smaller dose of toxin.

Christine Jenkins: Yes. Typically we say that if you smoke 20 cigarettes a day
for 20 years you're at risk of COPD, you've had enough exposure. But now we
know that women have a much reduced risk–exposure ratio, and so they need
only to smoke around five cigarettes a day for around 15 years…
 
Norman Swan: Five? As few as that?

Christine Jenkins: Indeed. And not only that, but the earlier they start smoking,
the more likely they are to develop COPD.

Norman Swan: And the symptomatology, if I remember rightly from my medical
school days we used to typify people as pink puffers and blue bloaters. Some
people have emphysema, some people have tight lungs—what happens in
women?

Christine Jenkins: The fancy terminology for that, Norman, although I must say
I still like those clinical phenotypes, is this concept of phenotypically driven
disease. So, different people have different types of presentation. And women
have a more airways disease type, that is cough and sputum rather than an
emphysema type. They may be prone to chest infections or prolonged symptoms
after a simple viral infection, for instance. And they're more likely to present with
what we call an exacerbation, a flare in their disease where they require a lot
more treatment, often steroids, antibiotics, and often even a hospital admission
because they haven't got enough oxygen in their blood and they need
supplementary oxygen.

Norman Swan: Now, it's often been said with heart disease in women, it's
ignored. People don't think that women get heart disease and therefore they're
diagnosed late and women contribute to that by sorting out everything to do with
the house before they actually go and see the doctor. Do people under-recognise
chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in women?

Christine Jenkins: Most definitely. In fact it's been traditionally thought that
COPD is a men's disease. More men smoke around the world, men are more
represented in clinical trials. So in therapeutic interventions we know a lot about
how men respond and not a lot about how women respond, because often
clinical trials have around 80% of the people in the trials are males. So women
have tended to be under-recognised, and often labelled as having asthma,
incorrectly diagnosed, or often they're sent off to the cardiologist.

Norman Swan: Because it's airways disease, the coughing and wheezing.
 
Christine Jenkins: Indeed, or they may not have smoked for the extent that
people expect you ought to have smoked in order to have this disease, and so
it's not top of mind when they see their GP. And therefore they don't get the right
treatment and they don't get the benefits of that.

Norman Swan: And they get more exacerbations and it's like a staircase going
down to death.

Christine Jenkins: Correct, because exacerbations contribute very substantially
to loss of lung function. So over time you lose your airway function such that your
breathing becomes more difficult, and you also lose the connection between your
alveolar spaces, your gas exchanging membranes, and the blood vessels that
wrap around them that help to transport oxygen.

Norman Swan: What's known about how you treat women as opposed to men?

Christine Jenkins: Well, we do know that women present earlier, so it's very
important to use that as the opportunity to make an accurate diagnosis, so
performing a lung function test, a breathing test is a really important thing. So if
you're breathless, please go to your doctor would be my message, and ask for a
breathing test. How you treat this disease is with a range of things that are non-
pharmacologic, things like physical activity, and we have really good exercise
programs for people with chronic lung disease. But also medications are very
effective in opening up the airways and reducing these exacerbation episodes.
And preventing infection is the other thing, vaccination against influenza in
particular.

Norman Swan: Christine, thank you very much indeed.

Christine Jenkins: Thank you, Norman.

Norman Swan: Christine Jenkins of the George Institute for Global Health in
Sydney.

I'm Norman Swan. This has been the Health Report and I hope you can join me
next week.

Norman Swan: Hello and welcome to this week's Health Report with me,
Norman Swann. Today there are 80,000 Australians who have an easily
diagnosed high genetic risk of cancer. They don't know it, and we need to do
something about it.

Ian Frayling: The little light comes on in your car with the oil light. Your airbus
will scream at you if you try to land with the wheels up, and your phone will tell
you when it's your anniversary tomorrow—it's life and death, right? So we have
to use technology simply to find these things and tell people what to do when
they need to do it.

Norman Swan: A world first for Australian research—a simple blood test, a so-
called liquid biopsy for cancer which saves having more expensive, painful and
less accurate tests.

How lung problems in women are different and doctors need to know about it, not
to mention women. And how you may not need to pay a fortune for brain training
programs to keep your mind fit. Some simple, cheap activities may be all you
need. At least according to a large study which has found a reduced instance of
what's called mild cognitive impairment, which can be the first step for some
people towards dementia. The lead author was Yonas Geda of the Mayo Clinic in
the United States.

Yonas Geda: Several groups of investigators, including ourselves, have reported
a cross-sectional association between mentally stimulating activities and
decreased odds of having mild cognitive impairment.

Norman Swan: And when you say cross-sectional, this means like a snapshot.

Yonas Geda: Yes.

Norman Swan: If you just take a snapshot in time, people who do mentally
stimulating activities seem to have better thinking and memory ability. But it
doesn't tell you whether or not it's cause and effect.

Yonas Geda: Exactly.

Norman Swan: So they could be doing these mentally stimulating activities
because they can rather than because it's helping them.

Yonas Geda: Exactly. So what we did is we published a cross-sectional study.
We looked at about ten mentally stimulating activities. We observed that five of
them are strongly associated with decreased odds of having MCI. So we took
those five…

Norman Swan: MCI being mild cognitive impairment.

Yonas Geda: Intermediate stage between normal ageing and dementia. So we
took those five mentally stimulating activities…

Norman Swan: What were they?

Yonas Geda: Reading books, playing games (when we say games, simple
games, board games), craft activities such as knitting, computer use (simple
email, browsing), and social activities. So we took these five and we tested it in a
prospective cohort study. We took about 2,000 people, 70 years and older.

Norman Swan: And just watched to see what happened to them…

Yonas Geda: Exactly. We followed them forward in time for an average of about
four years. And then we wanted to see…at baseline all of them are cognitively
normal, and then followed them forward in time and then tried to compare their
outcome of mild cognitive impairment between those who engage in mentally
stimulating activities versus those who don't.

Norman Swan: And what did you find?

Yonas Geda: Mentally stimulating activities, particularly craft activities, computer
use, social activities and playing games were associated with decreased risk of
having mild cognitive impairment.

Norman Swan: So this is the group as a whole…

Yonas Geda: Yes.

Norman Swan: And in fact when I look at your results, computer use really stood
out, the significance was much greater than the other activities.

Yonas Geda: Exactly. Computer use is top of the list, and again, we asked for
only simple computer use: email, browsing, that's it.

Norman Swan: And the social activities were what?

Yonas Geda: Doing group activities, going to theatres or going to a museum or
group activities such as Bible studying.

Norman Swan: Okay, so then you decided to look at it via genetic risk, using this
gene called APOE ε4, which does confer an increased risk of cognitive
impairment.

Yonas Geda: Particularly Alzheimer's. So we wanted to know, if I am a carrier of
the genetic risk, and if I still engage in reading books, I will have slightly
decreased risk of having MCI, even if I have genetic risk. Even if I have the
genetic risk, these mentally stimulating activities seem to confer some degree of
decreased risk for MCI as well.

Norman Swan: So what you're saying is then that these five activities—
particularly craft activities, computer use and social activities—those will protect
you to some extent if you're carrying this high risk gene.

Yonas Geda: 'To some extent' is a very good qualifier. If you don't have it, the
benefit is even more.

Norman Swan: So given that most people don't know their APOE ε4 status, the
bottom line is what?

Yonas Geda: The bottom line is that this paper, honestly, it gives hope. We
looked at very simple activities, accessible to anyone above age 70. We didn't
look at fancy gadgets, fancy games. And what we observed is that even if a
person starts mentally stimulating activities even in late life, after age 70 the
person starts these activities, there is reasonable chance to decrease the risk of
incident MCI by simply engaging in these accessible, simple mentally stimulating
activities.

Norman Swan: What sort of dose of these activities do people have to be doing?
Because if they were having an effect, more might be better. So how much of this
were they doing, and did you factor in—if you like to use a medical term—the
dose of these activities?

Yonas Geda: Anywhere from two days per week and then above we have
observed benefit.

Norman Swan: You mean twice a week for how long?

Yonas Geda: Even as small as twice a week for a year.

Norman Swan: On the computer for an hour a day, two hours a day—what?

Yonas Geda: Oh, actually unfortunately we didn't look at how many hours of
computer in one sitting. Unfortunately we didn't look at that one. But in general
we looked at number of activities per week. Engaging in any of these activities
about two times minimum per week seems to be associated with decreased risk.

Norman Swan: Yonas Geda, thank you very much for joining us on the Health
Report.

Yonas Geda: You are very welcome, and I look forward to listen to it.

Norman Swan: New listeners to the Health Report are always welcome. Yonas
Geda is Professor of Psychiatry and Neurology at the Mayo Clinic.

Eighty thousand Australians are estimated to have a genetic abnormality which
puts them at increased risk of a number of malignancies, especially bowel
cancer, and they don't know it. It's said that some carriers have up to a 75%
chance of developing cancer by the age of 70. It's called Lynch syndrome, and
as we speak, a report is being released calling for widespread testing. One of the
people involved is Ian Frayling, a British expert on Lynch syndrome, who's a
genetic pathologist at the University Hospital of Wales in Cardiff. I spoke to Ian
earlier.

Ian, thank you for joining us on the Health Report.

Ian Frayling: Pleasure.

Norman Swan: So 5% of people are actually only diagnosed with Lynch
syndrome. You'd better tell us the sort of cancers that Lynch syndrome's
associated with.

Ian Frayling: Well, it was first identified on the basis of predisposing to bowel
and endometrial, so that's womb cancer.

Norman Swan: Uterus.

Ian Frayling: Yeah, uterus, as well as to some extent gastric cancers like
stomach cancer. But it causes a whole variety, we now understand, about 12
different types and counting. There's a relatively low risk of ovarian cancer, but
also gall bladder, small bowel cancer, bile duct cancer, cancer of the ducts that
come down from the kidney, which is otherwise quite unusual. Young onset
bladder cancer, some brain cancers.

Norman Swan: So how would you know that there might be Lynch syndrome in
your family?

Ian Frayling: Well that's incredibly difficult for both professionals and members of
the public. Most people are familiar with familial breast/ovarian cancer, where it's
breast and ovary, largely.

Norman Swan: And in young women, relatively young women.

Ian Frayling: Yeah, it tends to occur in younger people.

Norman Swan: But that's true in Lynch syndrome as well.

Ian Frayling: That's true in Lynch…

Norman Swan: Are we talking about diagnosis under 50?

Ian Frayling: Well, about a third of cases of Lynch produce cancer below the age
of 50 in the bowel, about a third between 50 and 65, and a third over 65. So
you're never too young and you're never too old.

Norman Swan: So there's not really a reliable way of telling from your family
history.

Ian Frayling: No. It's more likely if it's younger, but it's not an absolute.

Norman Swan: And do you know, if you say to somebody, look bowel cancer
runs in my family. does that tell you if you're at risk?

Ian Frayling: That can do. The problem is that we've come at this from the
direction of spotting bowel cancer in families, but we now understand, because it
causes so many other cancers, that we can't be so selective. And in fact the
family history is useful but it's not the best way of finding it.

Norman Swan: And what's going wrong here, it's what's called a mismatch
repair gene, the DNA doesn't repair itself the way it would do in somebody who
doesn't have Lynch syndrome.

Ian Frayling: Yeah. The genes that are responsible for causing Lynch syndrome
are involved in the process of DNA repair in cells. And cells are very careful
things. They won't divide unless their DNA is repaired. So if you damage the
mechanism for mending DNA cells can divide in an unruly fashion. But there's
emerging evidence which is very exciting that perhaps there's another pathway to
cancer in Lynch syndrome hitherto undiscovered.

Norman Swan: Oh really, and that could end up with understanding better
treatments?

Ian Frayling: Absolutely. What all this study of familial bowel cancer in all its
different forms is telling us is that it's not a simple process. There's many different
ways to a bowel cancer.

Norman Swan: Now, the BRCA1 gene, breast cancer, is relatively rare, and it
follows ethnic groups like Ashkenazi Jews…or do you disagree with that?

Ian Frayling: Well, no, no, there are founder mutations for every genetic
condition on the planet.

Norman Swan: Once upon a time in the Ashkenazi Jewish population somebody
got that mutation and because it was in a closed community it spread.

Ian Frayling: Absolutely, kept it within themselves.

Norman Swan: And what about Lynch syndrome, is there any ethnic
identification, and is it that rare?

Ian Frayling: It's actually probably more common that familial breast/ovarian
cancer. It could be up to twice as common, but we get five times less referrals for

it than familial breast/ovarian. So there's a complete skewing against Lynch
syndrome because it's difficult to spot, members of the public find it difficult to
realise they're in a family situation, doctors don't understand it…

Norman Swan: But let's say you get the diagnosis, and we'll come to testing in a
moment, what do you do? Bowel cancer is fairly obvious, you can have regular
colonoscopies or faecal occult blood testing. But uterine cancer, biliary tract
cancer? These are not easy cancers to screen for or detect…

Ian Frayling: No.

Norman Swan: Is there a drug you can take that helps the mismatch?

Ian Frayling: We did a trial where we tried using aspirin in individuals with Lynch,
and it showed a remarkable result, that it seemed to be extremely effective at
preventing a large proportion of all the cancers they get, not just the bowel
cancers. We're now in the process of organising a trial around the world where
we're trying to find out the best dose of aspirin.

Norman Swan: Now, Monday evening, Australian time, launching a report which
calls for testing for Lynch syndrome. Who's going to get tested and how would
that happen, a screening program?

Ian Frayling: Hopefully in parallel with what the National Institute for Health and
Care Excellence in the UK has just authorised, which is that all bowel cancers in
the United Kingdom now must be tested to see if they're due to Lynch syndrome.
Based on the work we're doing at Cancer Council New South Wales, what we're
urging for is that a similar situation should pertain in Australia, and that when a
pathologist finds evidence of Lynch in a bowel cancer, which is done by a couple
of pretty standard tests now, that initiates a referral to the local clinical genetics
department, and the individual and their family can then be cared for
appropriately.

Norman Swan: So it's not the whole population, it's just that basically all bowel
cancer specimens should be tested for it and that's the red light that gets the
family tested and you can start doing what you have to do.

Ian Frayling: Yeah. It may also similarly be worth testing cases of endometrial
cancer and, for example, small bowel and gall bladder because they're so
characteristic.

Norman Swan: Can you afford it?

Ian Frayling: You can't afford not to do it. In the health economic analysis we did
in the UK, we showed that it was hugely worthwhile testing certainly the young
onset cases. It was worthwhile testing every case of bowel cancer up to the age
of 70, and NICE decided it was worth simply testing everybody. It was simpler to
advise that every bowel cancer get tested. If I can summarise a 500-page report
that we did in the UK down to a one-liner and trying to convert to Australian
dollars—you don't have to prevent many $65,000 bowel cancers to pay for a hell
of a lot of $100 tests and $500 colonoscopies.

Norman Swan: Ian Frayling, we'll watch this with interest. Thanks very much for
joining us.

Ian Frayling: Thank you Norman.

Norman Swan: And I must declare an interest in colorectal issues as the proud
owner of an occasional polyp. Ian Frayling is a genetic pathologist at the
University Hospital of Wales in Cardiff.

A liquid biopsy is like something out of Star Trek, an almost painless way to
diagnose disease without taking out large lumps of tissue surgically. A wife and
husband team at Peter MacCallum Cancer Centre in Melbourne have developed
a world first liquid biopsy for blood cancers like leukaemia, which may avoid
painful, expensive bone marrow biopsies. Sarah-Jane and Mark Dawson are in
our Melbourne studio. Welcome to the Health Report.

Sarah-Jane Dawson: Thank you for having us, Norman.

Mark Dawson: Thank you.

Norman Swan: Sarah, you were at Cambridge for ten years and you've now
decamped to the Palace on Parkville, the new Victorian Comprehensive Cancer
Centre.

Sarah-Jane Dawson: That's right, I'm from Melbourne originally, and did my
medical training here in Melbourne but then went to the University of Cambridge
and studied over there, did a PhD and some post-doctoral research over there,
and developed these skills that I've now brought back to Melbourne and more
specifically to Peter MacCallum Cancer Centre and the Victorian Comprehensive
Cancer Centre.

Norman Swan: Before we get to the blood cancers that you and Mark have
worked on, you yourself have developed liquid biopsies for solid tumours like
breast cancer. What is a liquid biopsy?

Sarah-Jane Dawson: Yes, so essentially a liquid biopsy is a test that measures
something called circulating tumour DNA. So we know that most cancer types
can actually release small, tiny fragments of cancer DNA into a patient's
bloodstream. And we now have quite sophisticated ways with which we can
measure these small amounts of circulating tumour DNA, and in doing so learn
something about the cancer and how it's responding to treatment.

Norman Swan: More than you can learn from a straight biopsy by putting the
needle in the tumour?

Sarah-Jane Dawson: Yes, so one of the advantages is this testing is based on a
blood test, so a blood test can certainly be repeated more frequently during
someone's cancer treatment compared to an invasive tissue biopsy. You know,
there are several limitations of tissue biopsies, they're invasive and quite
challenging for patients…

Norman Swan: You might miss the spot as well.

Sarah-Jane Dawson: That's right, yeah, they're only biopsy-ing a single area of
the tumour and we know that heterogeneity within cancers is a problem: no
single area of a tumour is the same. So the liquid biopsy alternative may be more
comprehensive. Certainly it allows us to see DNA that's been shed into the
bloodstream from all of the different sites of the tumour.

Norman Swan: Mark, tell us about this one for blood tumours. What are we
talking about here, leukaemia?

Mark Dawson: So the two major cancers that we've studied here are a disease
called chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, and another precursor condition called
myelodysplastic syndrome. So if we start with the latter, the latter is really a
problem of the production factory for our blood cells, which is the bone marrow.
And so…

Norman Swan: And you really teeter on a knife-edge of leukaemia when you've
got MDS.

Mark Dawson: Correct, that's exactly right, Norman. And really here the quality
and quantity of the cells that are being produced is not adequate. But this is
actually a relatively common disease that is quite difficult to diagnose, because
there are a number of different everyday exposures that may give rise to low
blood counts: infections, some of the toxins that we consume such as alcohol,
and other toxic exposures as well. So it's not always clear whether the low blood
counts are caused by a cancer. But all cancers, as you've just been talking
about, have a somatic or acquired mutation in their DNA. And essentially that's
what we look for, we look for an abnormality that says that the cells are
cancerous. We do that currently with a bone marrow biopsy, but what our results
suggest is that we may be able to do that effectively with the liquid biopsy.

Norman Swan: Sarah-Jane, tests have a chequered history; people tout them
with great hype and then you find that they're inaccurate. It depends on the
person who's doing the test whether or not you get a positive result or not.
They're horribly expensive and in the end may not tell you any more than you get
from the traditional test. How reliable and affordable are these liquid biopsies?

Sarah-Jane Dawson: This is not a new field. We've known for quite some time
that it's possible to find these small traces of cancer DNA in the bloodstream of
patients with cancer. But what's changed recently is improvement in technology.
We now have improvements in the way that we can reliably detect these small
amounts of DNA. So these tests are now much more sensitive than they have
been previously and this has really seen great growth and expansion of research
in this area.

Norman Swan: Are they ready for show time yet, or is it still experimental?

Sarah-Jane Dawson: We're certainly working very hard to now start to make
these tests more readily available for patients and we're hoping to be in a
situation to be able to do that in the next few months.

Norman Swan: And affordably?

Sarah-Jane Dawson: Yes. The costs of these tests are actually likely to be very
affordable for patients. They're still not covered by government subsidies but the
hope is in the future that the more patients that have access to these tests, then
they may actually be reimbursed.

Norman Swan: Mark, I want to talk to you about a paper you've just published
in Science magazine, one of the world's most prestigious journals—although you
and Sarah-Jane have also published in a very prestigious journal for your liquid
biopsy—on epigenetics and cancer and the opportunities for treatment we should
just talk about. So this is an extraordinary…it's not that new an area, but this is
stuff that happens around the outside of DNA rather than inside it itself.

Mark Dawson: That's right, Norman. So epigenetics I often describe using a very
common sight that is very familiar to everyone and that happens in nature; how a
caterpillar becomes a butterfly. These two look very, very different but essentially
their DNA, their blueprint…

Norman Swan: The genes are identical…

Mark Dawson: …it's absolutely identical. What is different is what pages of that
instruction manual are read to give rise to a caterpillar or a butterfly. And that
ability to be able to access the DNA at the right place at the right time, to be able
to repair it and replicate it, that process, and the proteins that control that
process, is the study of epigenetics.

Norman Swan: And to what extent is it involved in cancer?

Mark Dawson: What we've learned over the last ten years as we've been
sequencing lots of genomes of patients with cancer is that mutations in genes
that code for epigenetic regulators are probably the most frequently occurring
class of mutations in cancer. And this really shouldn't be…

Norman Swan: Just to be totally mind-bending, you're not talking about
mutations that directly cause the cancer, you're talking about mutations that
actually change the shape of the DNA and how it works.

Mark Dawson: No, it's a bit of both. So if we think of the proteins that change the
way we access our DNA we call these epigenetic proteins. The genes that code
for these epigenetic proteins are what is mutated in cancer. And this really makes
the genome much more plastic and more malleable, because when you mutate
these things you are suddenly able to keep genes on that should be turned off
with normal development. And similarly you sometimes turn off genes that would
come over to protect the cell, come on to protect a cell should something bad
happen. So mutations in epigenetic regulators are extremely common…

Norman Swan: So which kind of tumours are we talking about here?.

Mark Dawson: Virtually all tumours. Most tumours that've been sequenced have
been found to have mutations in epigenetic regulators.

Norman Swan: And what does it mean for treatment?

Mark Dawson: What it means for treatment is that we now have a new way of
trying to manipulate the cell, trying to rewire this cell by finding therapies that
target these mutated epigenetic regulators that turn off these genes in the
specific cancer cells and try to make them more susceptible to the body's way of
clearing them, including the immune system.

Norman Swan: Existing drugs, or new drugs?

Mark Dawson: New drugs. There is a raft of new drugs that are being developed
to try and tug at the epigenome to reset cancer cells.

Norman Swan: And will these work hand in hand with existing drugs, or do they
want to do the job by themselves?

Mark Dawson: It's very unlikely that they will do the job by themselves. They're
going to need to be used as part of combination therapies. And the next decade
will involve just working out how best to use them.

Norman Swan: So Sarah-Jane, does your liquid biopsy pick up epigenetic
changes, or just the throw-off DNA that's caused by cancer?

Sarah-Jane Dawson: No, it certainly can pick up epigenetic changes as well,
such as DNA methylation. So there is a whole host of genetic changes that
studying the cancer DNA in the bloodstream can reveal.

Norman Swan: Thank you very much to you both. Impressed, you know, a joint
husband and wife or wife and husband lab doing such great work,
congratulations.

Both: Thank you very much.

Norman Swan: Sarah-Jane and Mark Dawson, of the Peter MacCallum Cancer
Centre, and as I say, the Palace on Parkville, the new Victorian Comprehensive
Cancer Centre. If you're not from Melbourne you should drive by, it's a very
impressive building.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a massive chronic health issue
in Australia. The image that's usually portrayed is of a breathless man coughing
his lungs out. But women develop COPD too, and according to a paper last week
from the George Institute in Sydney, women with COPD receive scant attention,
despite being more likely to die from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease than
breast and lung cancer combined. And it also behaves differently in women. The
lead author was head of the George Institute Respiratory Group, respiratory
physician Christine Jenkins, and she's in our Sydney studio. Welcome, Christine.

Christine Jenkins: Good afternoon, Norman.

Norman Swan: So just tell us what COPD is, because I kind of glanced over
that, given that you know better than me.

Christine Jenkins: Yes, it's not a term people are familiar with, but they probably
are familiar with the words chronic bronchitis and emphysema. And they are
really the community's understanding of this disease. It's a chronic lung disease
where the airways narrow because the lung tissue is destroyed by gases, dusts,
particles, noxious inhalations of which tobacco smoke is the most common in our
country, but not in the rest of the world.

Norman Swan: Indoor cooking and that sort of thing, indoor fires can cause the
problem.

Christine Jenkins: Most definitely. Biomass fuel exposure, we call it, people
who have to burn carbon-rich fuel for their heating and cooking in poorly
ventilated houses around the world very commonly develop COPD as well. So
this accounts for why women globally actually have the same prevalence of
COPD as men, whilst in our country actually COPD is slightly more common in
men, but because women now smoke as much as men do it's becoming equal
and prevalent.

Norman Swan: And to what extent is it a problem, what's the dimension of
COPD in Australia?

Christine Jenkins: About 7% to 8% of people have significant COPD, clinically
important COPD. If you look at it over the age range it increases in prevalence
from the age of about 55 through to 80+, and by the time people are in their 80s
COPD prevalence be up around 15%.

Norman Swan: That's a lot of people.

Christine Jenkins: It's a large number of people. And in fact there's an epidemic
of COPD around the world, so around 300 million people around the world have
COPD. In 1990 it was the sixth leading cause of death from chronic disease. In
2000 it was the fourth and in 2020 it will be the third.

Norman Swan: And what's different about it in women?

Christine Jenkins: In women it is significantly different in a range of ways. The
first way, and one very important way for people to know is that women appear to
need a much smaller exposure to a noxious substance such as smoking in order
to develop COPD. So, for instance…

Norman Swan: So a bigger risk with a smaller dose of toxin.

Christine Jenkins: Yes. Typically we say that if you smoke 20 cigarettes a day
for 20 years you're at risk of COPD, you've had enough exposure. But now we
know that women have a much reduced risk–exposure ratio, and so they need
only to smoke around five cigarettes a day for around 15 years…

Norman Swan: Five? As few as that?

Christine Jenkins: Indeed. And not only that, but the earlier they start smoking,
the more likely they are to develop COPD.

Norman Swan: And the symptomatology, if I remember rightly from my medical
school days we used to typify people as pink puffers and blue bloaters. Some
people have emphysema, some people have tight lungs—what happens in
women?

Christine Jenkins: The fancy terminology for that, Norman, although I must say
I still like those clinical phenotypes, is this concept of phenotypically driven
disease. So, different people have different types of presentation. And women
have a more airways disease type, that is cough and sputum rather than an
emphysema type. They may be prone to chest infections or prolonged symptoms
after a simple viral infection, for instance. And they're more likely to present with
what we call an exacerbation, a flare in their disease where they require a lot
more treatment, often steroids, antibiotics, and often even a hospital admission
because they haven't got enough oxygen in their blood and they need
supplementary oxygen.

Norman Swan: Now, it's often been said with heart disease in women, it's
ignored. People don't think that women get heart disease and therefore they're
diagnosed late and women contribute to that by sorting out everything to do with
the house before they actually go and see the doctor. Do people under-recognise
chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in women?

Christine Jenkins: Most definitely. In fact it's been traditionally thought that
COPD is a men's disease. More men smoke around the world, men are more
represented in clinical trials. So in therapeutic interventions we know a lot about
how men respond and not a lot about how women respond, because often
clinical trials have around 80% of the people in the trials are males. So women
have tended to be under-recognised, and often labelled as having asthma,
incorrectly diagnosed, or often they're sent off to the cardiologist.

Norman Swan: Because it's airways disease, the coughing and wheezing.

Christine Jenkins: Indeed, or they may not have smoked for the extent that
people expect you ought to have smoked in order to have this disease, and so
it's not top of mind when they see their GP. And therefore they don't get the right
treatment and they don't get the benefits of that.

Norman Swan: And they get more exacerbations and it's like a staircase going
down to death.

Christine Jenkins: Correct, because exacerbations contribute very substantially
to loss of lung function. So over time you lose your airway function such that your
breathing becomes more difficult, and you also lose the connection between your
alveolar spaces, your gas exchanging membranes, and the blood vessels that
wrap around them that help to transport oxygen.

Norman Swan: What's known about how you treat women as opposed to men?

Christine Jenkins: Well, we do know that women present earlier, so it's very
important to use that as the opportunity to make an accurate diagnosis, so
performing a lung function test, a breathing test is a really important thing. So if
you're breathless, please go to your doctor would be my message, and ask for a
breathing test. How you treat this disease is with a range of things that are non-
pharmacologic, things like physical activity, and we have really good exercise
programs for people with chronic lung disease. But also medications are very
effective in opening up the airways and reducing these exacerbation episodes.
And preventing infection is the other thing, vaccination against influenza in
particular.

Norman Swan: Christine, thank you very much indeed.

Christine Jenkins: Thank you, Norman.

Norman Swan: Christine Jenkins of the George Institute for Global Health in
Sydney.

I'm Norman Swan. This has been the Health Report and I hope you can join me
next week.
